title: Africa's Oldest DNA Holds a Mystery
place: Grotte des Pigeons, Taforalt, Oriental Region, Morocco
text: About 15,000 years ago, Stone Age people began burying their dead at the back of Grotte des Pigeons, a cave near Taforalt. In 2018 scientists read nuclear DNA from these burials, the oldest yet recovered in Africa at the time. About two-thirds of the ancestry matched people then living in the Near East. The other third most resembled sub-Saharan Africans, yet no known population carries quite the same mix.

source.name: Max Planck Society: Scientists analyse oldest human DNA from Africa

title: Harpoon Fishers of a Brimming Lake
place: Lothagam, west shore of Lake Turkana, Turkana County, Kenya
text: When the Sahara was green, Lake Turkana stood far higher than today, and people at Lothagam lived along its shore. Digs in 1965 and 1966 turned up hundreds of barbed bone harpoon points and one of East Africa's largest collections of early Holocene human remains. Their pottery carried wavy-line patterns shared across the Sahara. Later drying cut the lake level by about half.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): New archaeological investigations at the Lothagam harpoon site at Lake Turkana

title: Paddling Across a Monster Current
place: Yonaguni Island, Okinawa, Japan (from eastern Taiwan)
text: About 30,000 years ago, people reached Japan's southern Ryukyu Islands by crossing the Kuroshio, one of the world's strongest ocean currents. To test how, a team built a 7.5-metre dugout and in 2019 paddled from Taiwan with no map, compass or GPS, steering by sun, stars and swells. They reached Yonaguni after 225 km and 45 hours. Simulations show success needed a smart launch point.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Traversing the Kuroshio: Paleolithic migration across one of the world's strongest ocean currents

title: Bare Feet Under a Canadian Beach
place: Calvert Island, British Columbia, Canada
text: In 2014, archaeologists digging under the sand of Calvert Island found a footprint about 60 cm down. Further digging exposed 29 prints pressed into clay about 13,000 years ago, when the sea stood 2 to 3 metres lower. Their sizes match at least three people, including a child, and toe marks show some went barefoot. Most faced up the beach, as if gathering around something.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Terminal Pleistocene epoch human footprints from the Pacific coast of Canada

title: When Zebras Grazed on Zanzibar
place: Kuumbi Cave, Jambiani, Zanzibar, Tanzania
text: During the Ice Age, low seas joined Zanzibar to mainland Africa. Hunters camping in Kuumbi Cave around 19,000 to 17,000 years ago brought home zebra, buffalo, waterbuck and reedbuck, animals that no longer live on the island, and broke the bones while fresh. As seas rose after about 12,000 years ago, the land bridge drowned, Zanzibar became an island, and the zebras slowly vanished.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Continental Island Formation and the Archaeology of Defaunation on Zanzibar, Eastern Africa

title: A Lone Footprint Beside a Mastodon
place: Pilauco site, Osorno, Los Lagos Region, Chile
text: Under the city of Osorno in southern Chile, excavators found a single print pressed into water-soaked ground about 15,600 years ago, near the skull of a gomphothere, an elephant relative. Volunteers stamped barefoot through matching mud to test it, and experts now assign the print to a human, most likely Homo sapiens. Monte Verde, another early site, lies only 100 km away.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): A late Pleistocene human footprint from the Pilauco archaeological site, northern Patagonia, Chile

title: The Americas' Oldest Dated Carved Figure
place: Lapa do Santo, Lagoa Santa Karst, Minas Gerais, Brazil
text: In July 2009, in the last days of a dig at Lapa do Santo, a limestone shelter in Brazil, excavators reached bedrock 4 metres down and found a tiny pecked figure. Just 30 cm tall, it shows a stick-like man with three-fingered hands, a C-shaped head and an oversized phallus. Buried by sediments at least 10,500 years old, it may be the oldest reliably dated figurative petroglyph in the Americas.

source.name: PLOS ONE (via PMC): Rock art at the Pleistocene/Holocene boundary in Eastern South America

title: Spear Points Older Than Clovis
place: Gault Site, Buttermilk Creek valley, central Texas, USA
text: At the Gault Site in central Texas, springs and fine chert drew people for thousands of years. Beneath a layer of famous Clovis tools, excavators found an older layer holding small stemmed and lanceolate spear points unlike anything Clovis. Luminescence dating of the sediments gave ages of about 16,000 to 20,000 years ago, suggesting Clovis spread among people who already lived across North America.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Evidence of an early projectile point technology in North America at the Gault Site, Texas, USA

title: A Cooking Pot from a Hunan Cave
place: Yuchanyan Cave, Daoxian County, Hunan, China
text: Ice Age foragers camping in Yuchanyan Cave, in southern China, left crumbly pieces of pottery among the bones of deer, boar, birds, tortoises and fish. One pot could be rebuilt: a pointed-bottomed cauldron 29 cm tall, with walls up to 2 cm thick, fired at only about 400 to 500 °C. Radiocarbon dates put the earliest sherds at roughly 18,000 years old, among the oldest pottery anywhere.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Radiocarbon dating of charcoal and bone collagen associated with early pottery at Yuchanyan Cave, Hunan Province, China

title: Stalking a Giant Sloth at White Sands
place: Alkali Flat, White Sands, New Mexico, USA
text: On the Alkali Flat at White Sands, a giant ground sloth's trackway twists and turns. Inside its footprints are more than ten human prints, left by someone stretching their stride to follow it while the tracks were still fresh. Where people appear, the sloth's path zigzags, and rings of claw marks show it rearing on its hind legs to defend itself. Researchers think humans were harassing or hunting it.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Footprints preserve terminal Pleistocene hunt? Human-sloth interactions in North America

title: A Clovis Baby Raised on Mammoth
place: Anzick site, near Wilsall, Montana, USA
text: Near Wilsall, Montana, a boy about 18 months old was buried with Clovis stone tools roughly 12,800 years ago. Because nursing babies carry their mother's chemical signature, scientists used isotopes in his bones to reconstruct her diet. The answer: mammoth probably made up 35 to 40 percent of what she ate, alongside deer or elk, bison or camel, and horse, with little sign of plant foods.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Mammoth featured heavily in Western Clovis diet

title: The Puzzling People of Maludong
place: Maludong (Red Deer Cave), near Mengzi, Yunnan, China
text: A thighbone dug up in 1989 at Maludong cave in Yunnan sits in layers about 14,000 years old. Its long neck and other features look archaic, and its owner weighed only about 50 kg, so a 2015 study suggested an archaic population had survived remarkably late. Later, ancient DNA from the cave instead pointed to an early, distinct branch of southern East Asian people.

source.name: PLOS ONE: A Hominin Femur with Archaic Affinities from the Late Pleistocene of Southwest China

source2.name: Genome Biology (via PMC): Ancient genomes give insight into 160,000 years of East Asian population dynamics

title: Volcanic Glass Carried 800 Kilometres
place: Shinbuk (Sinbuk) site, Jangheung County, South Jeolla, South Korea
text: At Shinbuk, near Korea's southern tip, Ice Age toolmakers left obsidian flakes and quartz crystals in a layer dated by charcoal to about 20,000 radiocarbon years ago. Chemical fingerprinting traced three flakes to Paektusan, the volcano on today's China–North Korea border, roughly 800 km away. Four others seem to come from Japan, making Shinbuk the only Korean Palaeolithic site known with Japanese obsidian.

source.name: Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association Bulletin 27: PIXE provenancing of obsidian artefacts from Paleolithic sites in Korea

title: Beads from a Giant Ostrich's Eggs
place: Shizitan, Jixian, Shanxi, China
text: On China's Loess Plateau, Ice Age people at Shizitan wore ornaments cut from the eggshell of Struthio anderssoni, an extinct giant ostrich. Across 14,000 years, 41 pieces show fashion changing: blackened pendants came first, then beads, some rubbed with red ochre. By the Younger Dryas cold snap, beads were made on site and shrank to about 4 mm across, drilled perhaps with tiny stone microblades.

source.name: Frontiers in Earth Science: Diachronic Change in the Utilization of Ostrich Eggshell at the Late Paleolithic Shizitan Site, North China

title: Japan's Ancestors Built for the Cold
place: Japanese archipelago (Jomon genomes from Kosaku shell mound, Funabashi, Chiba)
text: Japan's Jomon hunter-gatherers descend from a lineage that split from mainland East Asians about 27,000 to 19,000 years ago, around the coldest stretch of the Ice Age. A 2026 study of 42 Jomon genomes found variants in genes such as UCP1 and FTO, which help brown fat burn energy to make heat, plus a cold-sensing gene. Researchers see a legacy of that frozen past in people today.

source.name: Science Advances (via PMC): Jomon genomics reveal cold adaptation in Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers of eastern Eurasia

title: A Lone Skull from Kenya's Coldest Age
place: GvJm-22, Lukenya Hill, Athi-Kapiti Plain, Kenya
text: Dug up in the early 1970s on Lukenya Hill, a rocky outcrop above the plains of southern Kenya, a partial skull with a low, sloping forehead puzzled experts for decades. In 2015, 26 dates on ostrich eggshell placed it about 23,000 years ago, at the height of the last Ice Age. Its owner shared the hill with grindstones, ochre, eggshell beads and an extinct antelope.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Late Pleistocene age and archaeological context for the hominin calvaria from GvJm-22 (Lukenya Hill, Kenya)

title: Ice Age Campers Near 4,500 Metres
place: Cuncaicha rockshelter, Pucuncho Basin, Arequipa, Peru
text: High on Peru's treeless Andean plateau, Ice Age hunters made a base camp in Cuncaicha rockshelter, 4,480 metres above sea level, where air is thin and nights bitter. They sooted its ceiling with fires of cushion plants, left rock art, and ate vicuña, guanaco and taruca deer. Its oldest layers, about 12,400 years old, made it the highest Ice Age home known when reported in 2014.

source.name: EurekAlert! (University of Maine): Archaeologists document highest-altitude Ice Age human occupation

source2.name: University of Tübingen: Ice Age life high in the Andes

title: The Corridor That Opened Too Late
place: Ice-Free Corridor, northeastern British Columbia, Canada
text: For decades, textbooks said the first Americans walked south through a gap between two vast ice sheets in western Canada. Scientists sampled boulders and bedrock along 1,200 km of that route and measured beryllium made by cosmic rays since the ice melted. The corridor fully opened only about 13,800 years ago, after people were already living farther south, so the first travellers probably followed the Pacific coast.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): The age of the opening of the Ice-Free Corridor and implications for the peopling of the Americas

title: Horse and Camel on the Menu in Alberta
place: Wally's Beach, southern Alberta, Canada
text: At Wally's Beach in southern Alberta, hunters butchered seven horses and a camel, leaving 29 plain stone tools beside the bones. It is the only certain evidence that people in North America hunted these Ice Age animals. Twenty-seven radiocarbon dates on the bones show the kills all happened around 13,300 years ago, within a short span, not long before both species vanished from the continent.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Late Pleistocene horse and camel hunting at the southern margin of the ice-free corridor: reassessing the age of Wally's Beach, Canada

title: A Lake in the Karoo's Driest Corner
place: Grootvloer pan, Northern Cape, South Africa
text: Today Grootvloer in South Africa's Northern Cape is a dry, dusty pan. But freshwater mussel shells in its old shorelines date to about 21,000 years ago, at the peak of the last Ice Age, when a lake filled the basin. Along its edge lie bladelets and small cores left by Later Stone Age people, suggesting the interior was a magnet for life, not a barren waste.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Paleolakes and socioecological implications of last glacial greening of the South African interior

title: Gift Beads in the Lesotho Highlands
place: Sehonghong rock shelter, Thaba-Tseka District, Lesotho
text: Ostriches have never been known to live in highland Lesotho, yet Sehonghong shelter, 1,800 metres up, held 553 ostrich eggshell beads, some about 15,500 years old. Strontium in 27 beads showed most were made from eggs laid at least 109 km away, a few over 326 km away. Researchers see the beads as gifts swapped between distant groups, a safety net kept up for over 33,000 years.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Ostrich eggshell bead strontium isotopes reveal persistent macroscale social networking across late Quaternary southern Africa

title: Zebra Hunters of the Oujda Mountains
place: Rhafas Cave, Oujda Mountains, Oriental Region, Morocco
text: High in Morocco's Oujda Mountains, Rhafas Cave sheltered Stone Age hunters through the Ice Age. Most bones they left are from a North African zebra and wild ass, with some gazelle and hartebeest. A layer about 15,400 years old is dark with ash, a sign of busier fires and longer stays, as a warm spell spread forest across the region's highlands.

source.name: PLOS ONE: Expansion of forest cover and coeval shifts in Later Stone Age land-use at Taforalt and Rhafas Caves, Morocco

title: Clovis Hunters and Young Gomphotheres
place: El Fin del Mundo, Sonoran Desert, about 100 km northwest of Hermosillo, Sonora, Mexico
text: In 2007 a rancher in Mexico's Sonoran Desert reported bones and stone tools washing out of a gully wall. Excavators found two young gomphotheres, elephant relatives, with Clovis spear points lying among their bones, about 13,400 years old. It was the first evidence of Clovis people hunting gomphotheres, and one of the oldest and southernmost Clovis sites, hinting the culture began farther south than thought.

source.name: PNAS (via PMC): Human (Clovis)-gomphothere (Cuvieronius sp.) association about 13,390 calibrated yBP in Sonora, Mexico

title: Painters in an Amazon Cave
place: Caverna da Pedra Pintada, Monte Alegre, Pará, Brazil
text: Near Monte Alegre on the lower Amazon, the walls of Pedra Pintada cave carry red and yellow paintings of circles, crosses, frogs, snakes, fish, a manatee and human figures. Digging beneath one painted wall in 2014, archaeologists found people living there about 12,400 years ago, and a stone flake marked with paint in layers around 12,000 years old, suggesting painting began very early.

source.name: Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi (SciELO): The chronology of the cave paintings in the Pedra Pintada Cave, Monte Alegre, Pará

title: Sabretooth Bites on Pampas Giants
place: Salto de Piedra, Tapalqué Creek, near Olavarría, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
text: Sabre-toothed cats were long thought too fragile-toothed to bite through bone. Fossils at Salto de Piedra on Argentina's Pampas prove otherwise. Bones of toxodons, giant sloths, a glyptodont and a gomphothere, dated between about 22,000 and 13,000 years ago, carry grooves up to 33 mm wide gouged by Smilodon canines. The cat, up to about 400 kg, specialised in giants and was still hunting when the first people arrived nearby.

source.name: BMC Ecology and Evolution (via PMC): Smilodon sabertooth bite marks, new perspectives on prey-predator models in South American Pleistocene
